questions.stemText:
A light magnet is suspended inside a solenoid as shown in the figure below. The Earth’s magnetic flux density is $2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$ and the solenoid has 20 turns and a length of 15 cm. When a current is passed through the solenoid, it is found that the magnet rotates through an angle of $68^\circ$ from its original direction.

[Top view with N, E, S and W marked. The solenoid axis runs east–west. The upper row of winding cross-sections is marked with dots and the lower row with crosses. The magnet lies across the axis with its N pole pointing north.]

What is the value of the current flowing through the solenoid?

A 0.048 A
B 0.11 A
C 0.30 A
D 2.0 A

stemImage.alt: Question 24: A light magnet is suspended inside a solenoid as shown in the figure below. The Earth’s magnetic flux density is 2.0  10−5 T and the solenoid has 20 turns and

questions.difficultyReason: The student must obtain the solenoid field from the vector triangle before calculating the current.
questions.misconception: Confusing total turns with turns per metre

explanation.body: The Earth and solenoid fields are perpendicular, so $\tan68^\circ=B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}/B_{\mathrm{Earth}}$. Thus $B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}=(2.0\times10^{-5})\tan68^\circ=4.95\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$. Substituting into $B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}=\mu_0nI$ gives $4.95\times10^{-5}=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(20/0.15)I$, so $I=0.30\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the field components in the tangent ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the Earth’s field in place of the solenoid field.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses 20 turns per metre instead of 20 turns over 15 cm.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An electron is travelling in a vacuum at speed $v$. The electron enters a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$. A uniform electric field also exists in the region so that the electron remains undeflected and exits the region at point P as shown.

[In the shaded field region, magnetic field arrows point horizontally to the right. The electron enters from the lower left along a straight path sloping upwards to the right and exits at P on the top edge. The path makes angle $\theta$ with the horizontal magnetic field direction.]

The initial direction of the electron is at an angle of $\theta$ to the direction of the magnetic field.

What is the magnitude and direction of the electric field?

A. $Be\sin\theta$, into the page
B. $Be\sin\theta$, out of the page
C. $Bv\sin\theta$, into the page
D. $Bv\sin\theta$, out of the page

stemImage.alt: Question 25: An electron is travelling in a vacuum at speed v. The electron enters a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density B. A uniform electric field also exists

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must balance the force magnitudes and reverse the direction of the electric force to find the field.
questions.misconception: Confusing the electric force direction with the field direction for an electron

explanation.body: The magnetic force on the electron points out of the page and has magnitude $F_B=Bev\sin\theta$. To keep the electron undeflected, the electric force must have the same magnitude, so $E=F_E/e=Bv\sin\theta$. The electric force points into the page, so the electric field points out of the page because the electron is negatively charged.

perOption.A: Keeps the charge rather than the speed in the field magnitude and reverses the required field direction.
perOption.B: Keeps the charge rather than the speed after dividing the magnetic force by $e$.
perOption.C: Assigns the electric force direction to the field even though the electron is negatively charged.
perOption.D: Correct. The field is $Bv\sin\theta$ out of the page.

[Square PQRS has P at the upper left, Q at the upper right, R at the lower right and S at the lower left. An arrow at the centre O points to the right and is labelled resultant magnetic field.]

Due to the current in the four conductors, the resultant magnetic field at O is in the direction shown.

Which of the following must be the directions of the currents in each of the four conductors?

Option | into the page | out of the page
A | P, Q | R, S
B | P, S | Q, R

The diagram shows a bent wire in a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$.

The length of wire in the field is $L$ and each half of the wire is inclined at an angle $\theta$ normal to the field direction. There is a current $I$ in the wire.

[Horizontal magnetic field lines point right. The current follows a bent wire from top to bottom. Two segments of length $L/2$ meet at a bend to the left of the dashed vertical line joining the entry and exit points. Each segment makes angle $\theta$ with that vertical line.]

Which row gives the magnitude and the direction of the force acting on the wire?

[Table columns in order: magnitude, direction.]

B $BIL\cos\theta$, into the page
C $BIL\sin\theta$, out of the page

questions.misconception: Using the angle to the normal directly in the sine form of the force equation.

explanation.body: Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a force out of the page. As $\theta$ tends to $0^\circ$, the wire becomes perpendicular to the field and the force is greatest. Each half contributes a perpendicular length $(L/2)\cos\theta$, so $F=BI(2)(L/2)\cos\theta=BIL\cos\theta$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two parallel, straight conductors, placed at right angles to a ruler, carry currents of 2I and I

At which point on the ruler is the resultant magnetic field the greatest?
questions.stemText: Two parallel, straight conductors, placed at right angles to a ruler, carry currents of 2I and I flowing in opposite directions. 2I I At which point on the ruler is the resultant magnetic field the greatest? A 20 cm mark B 40 cm mark C 50 cm mark D 70 cm mark
questions.difficultyReason: The student must find field directions and compare the sums at different distances from the two wires.
questions.misconception: Adding field magnitudes where the fields oppose

explanation.body: By the right-hand grip rule, the fields add between the wires and oppose outside them. At the $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark, $B=\frac{\mu_0(2I)}{2\pi(0.10)}+\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(0.20)}=\frac{12.5\mu_0 I}{\pi}$. At the $50\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark, $B=\frac{\mu_0(2I)}{2\pi(0.20)}+\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(0.10)}=\frac{10\mu_0 I}{\pi}$. The greatest resultant is at $40\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: The weaker wire’s field opposes the stronger wire’s field at 20 cm.
perOption.B: Correct. The fields reinforce and the stronger wire is closer.
perOption.C: The fields reinforce, but the nearer wire carries the smaller current.
perOption.D: The two fields oppose at 70 cm, where the closer wire carries the smaller current.

questions.misconception: Using the field’s angle to the horizontal as its angle to the current.

explanation.body: In the selector, $B_1qv=qE$, so both ions emerge with speed $v=E/B_1$. In the second field, the magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $B_2qv=mv^2/r$, so $r=mv/(qB_2)=mE/(qB_1B_2)$. perOption.B: Inverts the combined mass-to-charge ratio for Q relative to P.

explanation.body:

Four parallel current carrying conductors are placed vertically at the corners of a square WXYZ. The magnitudes of the current at W and X are $I$ while the magnitudes of the current at Y and Z are $2I$.

[Square with W at the top left, X at the top right, Y at the bottom right and Z at the bottom left. A vertical arrow points down from O, midway along WX.]

O is the mid-point between W and X. If there is to be a resultant magnetic flux density produced at O in the direction shown, which option gives the largest magnetic flux density?

Option | Current into the plane | Current out of the plane
A | W and Z | X and Y
B | X and Z | W and Y
C | W and Y | X and Z
D | X and Y | W and Z

stemImage.alt: Question 23: Four parallel current carrying conductors are placed vertically at the corners of a square WXYZ. The magnitudes of the current at W and X are I while the magnit

questions.difficultyReason: The student must determine four field directions and resolve and combine their components.
questions.misconception: Adding magnetic flux densities as scalars.

explanation.body: Let $d$ be the side of the square and $K=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)$. W and X are each $d/2$ from O, giving a field of magnitude $2K$ each, while Y and Z are each $\sqrt{5}d/2$ from O and give $4K/\sqrt{5}$ each. The fields from Y and Z are tangential about their respective wires, so each has a component perpendicular to WX of magnitude $(4K/\sqrt{5})(1/\sqrt{5})=4K/5$. With W and Z into the plane and X and Y out, all four vertical contributions point down and the horizontal components cancel.

perOption.A: Correct. All four downward contributions reinforce.
perOption.B: The upward fields from W and X outweigh the downward components from Y and Z.
perOption.C: The upward components from Y and Z partly cancel the downward fields from W and X.
perOption.D: All four vertical contributions point upward.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An electron P, having a speed $v$, travels at right-angles to a uniform magnetic field. P then travels in a circular orbit of period $T$ and orbital radius $r$.

Another electron Q travels at right-angles to the same magnetic field. Q travels in a circular orbit of radius $2r$. What are the period and speed of Q?

Option | Period | Speed
A | $2T$ | $v$
B | $0.5T$ | $v$
C | $T$ | $2v$
D | $T$ | $0.5v$

stemImage.alt: Question 24: An electron P, having a speed v, travels at right-angles to a uniform magnetic field. P then travels in a circular orbit of period T and orbital radius r. Anoth

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine magnetic and centripetal force and identify what determines the period.
questions.misconception: Assuming a longer orbit always takes longer.

explanation.body: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, so $B|q|v=mv^2/r$ and $r=mv/(B|q|)$. Since $\omega=v/r=B|q|/m$, the period is $T=2\pi m/(B|q|)$. Both electrons have the same $m$, $|q|$ and $B$, so Q has speed $2v$ at radius $2r$ and the same period $T$.

perOption.A: Doubling the circumference would double the period at fixed speed, but the speed also doubles.
perOption.B: The speed cannot stay fixed when the radius doubles, and the period is independent of the radius.
perOption.C: Correct. The radius and speed double together.
perOption.D: The radius is directly proportional to speed, so the speed doubles.

questions.stemText:
The diagram shows a V-shaped wire in the magnetic field of flux density $B$. The length of the wire in the field is $L$ and the first half of the wire is inclined with an angle $\theta$ normal to the field direction. The current in the wire is $I$.

[The uniform magnetic field points right. The wire runs down from the upper endpoint, diagonally down-left to the vertex, then diagonally down-right to the lower endpoint. Both sloping segments are labelled $L/2$ and make angle $\theta$ with the dashed vertical line joining the endpoints. Current arrows point down at both endpoints.]

Which row gives the magnitude and direction of the force acting on the wire?

Option | Magnitude | Direction
A | $BIL\cos\theta$ | into of the page
B | $BIL\cos\theta$ | out of the page
C | $BIL\sin\theta$ | into the page
D | $BIL\sin\theta$ | out of the page

stemImage.alt: Question 25: The diagram shows a V-shaped wire in the magnetic field of flux density B. The length of the wire in the field is L and the first half of the wire is inclined w

questions.difficultyReason: The student must project both wire segments and apply Fleming’s left-hand rule.
questions.misconception: Using the angle to the normal as the angle to the field.

explanation.body: The components of both halves perpendicular to the field point down, giving $F=BI[(L/2)\cos\theta+(L/2)\cos\theta]=BIL\cos\theta$. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a force out of the page.

perOption.A: Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the opposite direction.
perOption.B: Correct. Both perpendicular components contribute to the outward force.
perOption.C: The sine projects onto the field direction, and the force direction is reversed.
perOption.D: The sine projects onto the field direction, which contributes no force.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Electrons, each of mass $m$ and charge $q$, are accelerated from rest in a vacuum through a potential difference $V$.

The accelerated electrons are then projected at point S into a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$, as shown. The electrons move in a circular path of radius $r$.

[The electrons travel vertically down to S at the upper boundary of the shaded field region, then follow a dashed semicircular path of radius $r$ curving to the left within the region.]

Which of the following expressions represents the specific charge $\frac{q}{m}$ of the electrons?

A $\frac{V}{2B^2r}$
B $\frac{2V}{B^2r}$
C $\frac{V}{2B^2r^2}$
D $\frac{2V}{B^2r^2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 24: Electrons, each of mass m and charge q, are accelerated from rest in a vacuum through a potential difference V. The accelerated electrons are then projected at

questions.difficultyReason: Requires linking the energy gain to magnetic circular motion and eliminating speed.
questions.misconception: Failing to square the radius when eliminating speed

explanation.body: Taking $q$ as the charge magnitude, the energy gain gives $qV=\tfrac12 mv^2$, so $v=\sqrt{2qV/m}$. The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, $Bqv=mv^2/r$. Substituting the energy expression gives $\sqrt{2qV/m}=2V/(Br)$. Squaring and rearranging gives $q/m=2V/(B^2r^2)$.

perOption.A: This leaves the radius unsquared and puts the factor of two in the denominator.
perOption.B: This leaves the radius unsquared when squaring the expression for speed.
perOption.C: This puts the factor of two from the kinetic-energy equation in the denominator.
perOption.D: Correct. Eliminating speed gives the stated charge-to-mass magnitude.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A narrow parallel beam of charged particles, each with speed $v$, passes through a slit $S_1$ into an evacuated region, moving in the direction towards slit $S_2$.

The evacuated region is shown shaded on the diagram.

[Particles enter the shaded region horizontally from the left through slit $S_1$ at speed $v$. Slit $S_2$ is on the right at the same height, and the arrow for the uniform electric field $E$ points vertically downwards.]

Uniform magnetic and electric fields are applied in the same evacuated region, with the electric field $E$ in the direction shown. The particles continue to exit through slit $S_2$.

What is the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field?

Option | magnitude | direction
A | $\frac{E}{v}$ | into the plane of the paper
B | $\frac{E}{v}$ | out of the plane of the paper
C | $Ev$ | into the plane of the paper
D | $Ev$ | out of the plane of the paper

stemImage.alt: Question 23: A narrow parallel beam of charged particles, each with speed v, passes through a slit S1 into an evacuated region, moving in the direction towards slit S2. The

questions.difficultyReason: The student must balance the forces and check which magnetic-field direction produces the required opposing force.
questions.misconception: Choosing fields without checking the directions of the forces

explanation.body: The beam passes undeflected, so the electric and magnetic forces balance: $B|q|v=|q|E$, giving $B=E/v$ for a perpendicular field. For a positive charge moving right, a field into the page gives an upward magnetic force to balance the downward electric force. Both forces reverse for a negative charge.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: A field out of the page makes the magnetic force reinforce the electric force.
perOption.C: The direction is correct, but balancing the forces requires dividing $E$ by $v$.
perOption.D: Multiplies by $v$ and reverses the field direction needed for cancellation.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two long straight wires X and Y are placed perpendicular to each other at a distance $d$ apart. A current flows out of the page in wire X. The same current flows from left to right in wire Y.

What are the directions of the forces acting on wire Y at the point P and Q due to the magnetic field produced by wire X?

[Wire Y lies horizontally with current $I$ to the right. Wire X is shown end-on with a dot, a perpendicular distance $d$ above Y. P and Q lie on Y to the left and right of X respectively.]

Option | force at P | force at Q
A | out of page | into page
B | into page | out of page
C | towards X | away from X
D | towards X | towards X

stemImage.alt: Question 23: Two long straight wires X and Y are placed perpendicular to each other at a distance d apart. A current flows out of the page in wire X. The same current flows

questions.difficultyReason: Requires combining the right-hand grip rule with Fleming’s left-hand rule at two points.
questions.misconception: Applying parallel-wire attraction rules to perpendicular wires

explanation.body: The right-hand grip rule gives an anticlockwise magnetic field around X, with a downward component at P and an upward component at Q. Applying Fleming’s left-hand rule to the rightward current in Y gives a force into the page at P and out of the page at Q.

perOption.A: Reverses the force directions at both points.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treats the force as radial to X, although it must be perpendicular to the current in Y.
perOption.D: Applies the attraction rule for parallel currents to perpendicular wires.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A square coil of 10 turns with sides of 5.0 cm is placed so that the plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the direction of a uniform magnetic field B of flux density 2.0 T. A current of 15 A is passed through the coil.

What is the magnitude of the torque acting on the square coil?
questions.stemText: A square coil of 10 turns with sides of 5.0 cm is placed so that the plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the direction of a uniform magnetic field B of flux density 2.0 T. A current of 15 A is passed through the coil. plane of coil 30° B = 2.0 T What is the magnitude of the torque acting on the square coil? A 0.19 N m B 0.33 N m C 0.38 N m D 0.65 N m
questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify the magnetic couple and project the coil width to find the perpendicular separation.
questions.misconception: Using the coil angle to project the wrong lever arm.

explanation.body: The opposite magnetic forces on the two sides form a couple with perpendicular separation $d=L\cos30^\circ$. With $N$ turns, the torque is $\tau=NBILd=10(2.0)(15)(5.0/100)(5.0/100)\cos30^\circ\approx0.65\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the sine projection and halves the couple's torque again.
perOption.B: Uses half the perpendicular separation while counting only one force.
perOption.C: Uses the sine projection for the separation of the forces.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two long, straight, current-carrying wires, X and Y are at a perpendicular distance 5.0 m apart. The current in X is 3.0 A and into the plane of the paper, while current in Y of 6.0 A is towards the top of the page. Point P is on the line of shortest distance joining the two wires, at a distance 2.0 m away from wire X as shown. [Diagram: wire X shown end-on with current 3.0 A into the page; wire Y drawn vertically in the plane of the page 5.0 m to the right with 6.0 A upward; P lies on the horizontal line between them, 2.0 m from X.] What is the magnitude of the resultant magnetic flux density at point P? A $3.5\times10^{-12}$ T B $5.0\times10^{-7}$ T C $6.3\times10^{-7}$ T D $7.0\times10^{-7}$ T

stemImage.alt: Question 24: Two long, straight, current-carrying wires, X and Y are at a perpendicular distance 5.0 m apart. The current in X is 3.0 A and into the plane of the paper, whil

questions.difficultyReason: Needs fields from two wires and recognising the two contributions are perpendicular.
questions.misconception: Adding or subtracting the two fields as if parallel

explanation.body: Using $B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)$, wire X gives $3.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$ towards the bottom of the page at $d=2.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Wire Y gives $4.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$ out of the page at $d=3.0\ \mathrm{m}$. The fields are perpendicular, so $B_{\mathrm{resultant}}=\sqrt{(3.0\times10^{-7})^2+(4.0\times10^{-7})^2}=5.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\varepsilon_0$ in place of $\mu_0$.
perOption.B: Correct. The fields add at right angles.
perOption.C: Swaps the distances from P to wires X and Y.
perOption.D: Adds the field magnitudes directly as if the fields were parallel.

What is the direction of the force acting on wire P?

[P is at the rightmost vertex of a regular hexagon. The leftmost wire carries current out of the page. All other wires, including P, carry current into the page. The arrows from P are A up, B right, C down and D left.]

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish attraction from repulsion and use symmetry and distance to find the net force.
questions.misconception: Opposite currents attract.

explanation.body: Four wires carry current in the same direction as P and attract it towards the left. Their vertical components cancel in pairs. The furthest wire carries opposite current and repels P to the right, but its force is weaker than the combined leftward components, so the net force points left.

perOption.A: Keeps an upward component even though the vertical components cancel by symmetry.
perOption.B: Lets the distant wire’s repulsion outweigh the four wires’ combined leftward attraction.
perOption.C: Keeps a downward component even though the vertical components cancel by symmetry.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Fig. (a) shows the top view of two long parallel wires, wire X and wire Y, carrying currents $I_X$ and $I_Y$ respectively in a direction perpendicular to the plane of the paper. The distance between wire X and wire Y is $L$.

Fig. (b) shows the variation of the net magnetic field at distances to the right of wire Y along the line joining wire X and wire Y. At a distance $d$ from wire Y, the net magnetic field is zero.

[Fig. (a), top view (not to scale): X lies to the left of Y on a dashed horizontal line, and their separation is marked $L$. Fig. (b): The vertical axis gives net magnetic field and the horizontal axis gives distance from wire Y. The curve rises from a negative field through zero at $d$ and continues upwards with decreasing slope.]

Given that the ratio $I_X/I_Y$ is 4.00 and taking the upwards direction to be positive, which of the following gives the relative direction of $I_X$ and $I_Y$ and the value of $L$ in terms of $d$?

A $I_X$ and $I_Y$ flow in opposite directions | $d$
B $I_X$ and $I_Y$ flow in the same direction | $d$
C $I_X$ and $I_Y$ flow in opposite directions | $3d$
D $I_X$ and $I_Y$ flow in the same direction | $3d$

stemImage.alt: Question 23: Fig. (a) shows the top view of two long parallel wires, wire X and wire Y, carrying currents IX and IY respectively in a direction perpendicular to the plane of

appearances.originalFile: grail:16192 2018 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Infers opposite field directions at the zero crossing and uses the distance to each wire in the field equation.
questions.misconception: Using the distance from Y for both wires

explanation.body: At distance $d$ from Y, the net field is zero, so the fields have equal magnitudes and opposite directions. On the same side of both wires, this requires opposite currents. Equating the field magnitudes gives $\mu_0 I_X/[2\pi(L+d)]=\mu_0 I_Y/(2\pi d)$, so $(L+d)/d=I_X/I_Y=4.00$ and $L=3d$.

perOption.A: With $L=d$ the distances are in a ratio of two, so the fields cannot balance for a current ratio of four.
perOption.B: Same-direction currents give reinforcing fields there, and $L=d$ gives the wrong distance ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Same-direction currents produce fields that add to the right of both wires.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A high energy particle which carries no charge enters a region of uniform magnetic field directed into the paper. The particle subsequently disintegrates to form two particles X and Y which have the same mass and same magnitude of charge.

The paths of X and Y are shown in the diagram and the initial radius of Y is twice the initial radius of X.

[Inside the uniform magnetic field directed into the paper, a dashed horizontal track enters from the left and splits into two inward spirals. X curves upwards into the smaller spiral, and Y curves downwards into the larger spiral.]

Which of the following statements is correct?

A Particle X is negatively charged, particle Y is positively charged.
B The ratio of the initial kinetic energy of particle X to particle Y is 0.25.
C The speeds of both particles are increasing steadily.
D Particle X has a larger momentum than particle Y.

stemImage.alt: Question 24: A high energy particle which carries no charge enters a region of uniform magnetic field directed into the paper. The particle subsequently disintegrates to for

appearances.originalFile: grail:16192 2018 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Relates magnetic curvature to speed and then squares the speed ratio to compare kinetic energies.
questions.misconception: Treating kinetic energy as proportional to track radius

explanation.body: Because X and Y have the same mass-to-charge-magnitude ratio, $r=mv/(|q|B)$ makes the speed ratio equal to the radius ratio. For equal masses, $K_X/K_Y=(v_X/v_Y)^2=(r_X/r_Y)^2=(1/2)^2=0.25$.

perOption.A: Reverses the charge signs indicated by the initial curvature: X is positive and Y is negative.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The shrinking radii indicate decreasing speeds, and the magnetic force itself does no work.
perOption.D: The smaller radius gives X the smaller momentum for equal charge magnitudes.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
MN and PQ are the upper and the lower sides of a rectangular conductor, respectively. An electric current is passed through the conductor, which is fixed in position, and placed in a uniform magnetic field pointing out of the plane of the paper as shown. This results in a potential difference between MN and PQ.

[A horizontal rectangular conductor carries current to the right. A shaded central region shows a uniform magnetic field out of the plane. M and N mark the upper edge of the conductor at the left and right of the field region, and P and Q mark the lower edge.]

The current may be due to the flow of either positive or negative charge carriers.

Which side, MN or PQ, in each case, is at a higher potential?

Option | Positive charge carriers | Negative charge carriers
A | MN | MN
B | MN | PQ
C | PQ | MN
D | PQ | PQ

stemImage.alt: Question 23: MN and PQ are the upper and the lower sides of a rectangular conductor, respectively. An electric current is passed through the conductor, which is fixed in pos

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine carrier drift direction, magnetic deflection and the sign of the accumulated charge.
questions.misconception: Taking electron drift to be in the direction of conventional current

explanation.body: Positive carriers move with the current and negative carriers move against it. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a downward magnetic force in both cases, so the carriers accumulate at PQ. Positive carriers make PQ higher in potential, while negative carriers make PQ lower, leaving MN higher.

perOption.A: Positive carriers accumulate at PQ and make it higher in potential.
perOption.B: Both carrier types deflect towards PQ, where positive carriers raise the potential and negative carriers lower it.
perOption.C: Correct. The sign of the charge accumulating at PQ determines which side is higher.
perOption.D: Negative carriers accumulating at PQ make MN the higher-potential side.

questions.stem:

Which of the following independent changes leaves the magnitude of the magnetic force on the wire unchanged?

The magnetic field acts along the y-axis into the plane of the paper. z wire current x uniform magnetic field acting into the paper Which of the following independent changes leaves the magnitude of the magnetic force on the wire unchanged? A Increase the current B Increase the flux density C Rotate the wire about the x-axis D Rotate the wire about the y-axis

options.label: C
options.text: Rotate the wire about the x-axis

options.label: D

questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify which rotation preserves the angle between the wire and the field.
questions.misconception: Confusing the field axis with an axis perpendicular to it

explanation.body: Rotation about the $y$-axis keeps the wire perpendicular to the magnetic field. Rotation about the $x$-axis changes the perpendicular component of the wire’s length during the rotation, changing the force magnitude.

perOption.A: A larger current increases the force magnitude.
perOption.B: A larger magnetic flux density increases the force magnitude.
perOption.C: This rotation tilts the wire towards the field and generally reduces the perpendicular length.
perOption.D: Correct. The wire stays perpendicular to the field.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A coil Q of a single turn and radius $r$, carries an anti-clockwise current $I_Q$ and lies flat on the table. A long straight wire P carrying current $I_P$ is placed on the same table such that its perpendicular distance from the centre of coil Q is $2r$.

[Wire P is drawn horizontally above coil Q. The distance from the wire to the top of the coil is $r$, and that point is another $r$ from the coil centre. An arrow on the right of Q shows the anti-clockwise current $I_Q$.]

Which of the following will cause the resultant magnetic field at the centre of coil Q to be zero?

A. $I_P$ to the right, $I_P=2\pi I_Q$
B. $I_P$ to the left, $I_P=2\pi I_Q$
C. $I_P$ to the right, $I_Q=2\pi I_P$
D. $I_P$ to the left, $I_Q=2\pi I_P$

stemImage.alt: Question 25: A coil Q of a single turn and radius r , carries an anti-clockwise current IQ and lies flat on the table. A long straight wire P carrying current IP is placed o

appearances.originalFile: grail:16202 2020 RI Prelims H2 Phy Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: It requires equating two field formulas and determining the current direction separately.
questions.misconception: Reversing the current ratio or wire field direction.

explanation.body:
The single turn gives $B_Q=\mu_0I_Q/(2r)$ at its centre, and the wire gives $B_P=\mu_0I_P/[2\pi(2r)]$ there. Cancellation requires equal, opposite fields, so $B_Q=B_P$ in magnitude gives $I_Q=I_P/(2\pi)$ and hence $I_P=2\pi I_Q$.

The coil’s field is out of the page, so the wire’s field must be into the page at the coil centre. This requires a current to the right.

perOption.A: Correct. The two fields are equal and opposite.
perOption.B: A leftward current makes the wire's field reinforce the coil's field.
perOption.C: The direction is right but the current ratio is inverted.
perOption.D: The ratio is inverted and the wire's field reinforces the coil's field.

questions.misconception: Reversing the potential polarity of the electron-rich edge.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A current balance consists of a U-shaped wire frame of length 15 cm and breadth 6.0 cm.

3.0 cm of the wire is in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 60 mT.

When the switch is open, the current balance is horizontal and in equilibrium when a paper rider of mass 5.0 g is placed at 2.5 cm to the right of the pivot as shown in the diagram.

When the switch is closed, the current balance is in equilibrium when the same paper rider is placed 6.8 cm to the right of the pivot.

What is the value of the current in the wire when the switch is closed?
questions.stemText: A current balance consists of a U-shaped wire frame of length 15 cm and breadth 6.0 cm. 3.0 cm of the wire is in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 60 mT. When the switch is open, the current balance is horizontal and in equilibrium when a paper rider of mass 5.0 g is placed at 2.5 cm to the right of the pivot as shown in the diagram. When the switch is closed, the current balance is in equilibrium when the same paper rider is placed 6.8 cm to the right of the pivot. paper rider 2.5 cm 15 cm 3.0 cm 6.0 cm S N pivot What is the value of the current in the wire when the switch is closed? A 1.2 A B 3.9 A C 7.8 A D 12 A

appearances.originalFile: grail:16209 2021 RI Prelims H2 Phy Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student finds the change in the rider's moment and uses the correct force length and lever arm.
questions.misconception: Using the whole wire segment as the length in the field

explanation.body: For the frame to remain horizontal, the magnetic torque must equal the extra torque from moving the rider. With $F=BIL$, the balance is $(60\times10^{-3})I(3.0/100)(15/100)=(5.0/1000)(9.81)(4.3/100)$, where $4.3=6.8-2.5$. This gives $I=7.81\ \mathrm A$.

perOption.A: At $1.2\ \mathrm A$ the magnetic torque is too small to balance the extra torque from moving the rider.
perOption.B: Using the $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ frame breadth as the length in the field halves the calculated current.
perOption.C: Correct. The magnetic torque balances the extra moment from shifting the rider.
perOption.D: Using the full $6.8\ \mathrm{cm}$ rider distance instead of its $4.3\ \mathrm{cm}$ shift overestimates the magnetic torque required.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Three long vertical wires P, Q and R are carrying currents $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$, $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$, respectively. The diagram shows the top view of the wires with the directions of their currents and the distances between them. perOption.B: Uses the r.m.s. current in the peak-field calculation.

perOption.A: Uses the whole side length $p+q$ as the length of wire in the field.
perOption.B: Uses the full side length $p+q$ and substitutes mass for weight.
perOption.C: Correct. The weight and magnetic force produce equal opposing moments.
perOption.D: Omits $g$ when converting the hanging mass to weight.

[The two horizontal arms join at their right ends via a vertical crosspiece $0.093\ \mathrm{m}$ long. The vertical pivot crosses the arms $0.23\ \mathrm{m}$ left of the crosspiece. The U-shaped wire experiences a turning moment about the pivot of value $4.7\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.

What is the magnitude of the magnetic flux density of the constant magnetic field?

A $5.27\ \mathrm{mT}$
B $22.9\ \mathrm{mT}$
C $45.8\ \mathrm{mT}$
D $4.37\ \mathrm{T}$

explanation.body: The magnetic force on the $0.093\ \mathrm{m}$ crosspiece is $F_B=BIL\sin\theta$, with $\theta=90^\circ$. Its moment about the pivot is $F_Bd=4.7\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{N\,m}$, using $d=0.23\ \mathrm{m}$. Thus $B=4.7\times10^{-6}/[(9.6\times10^{-3})(0.093)\sin90^\circ(0.23)]=22.9\ \mathrm{mT}$.

explanation.body:
Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the conventional current is from X to Y. Electron flow is opposite to conventional current, so electrons flow from Y to X.

questions.stemText: Two long, parallel, straight wires X and Y carry equal currents into the plane of the page as shown. The diagram shows arrows representing the magnetic flux density B at the position of each wire and the magnetic force F on each wire. (magnetic flux density at X due to Y) (magnetic flux density at Y due to X) The current in wire Y is doubled. Which diagram best represents the magnetic flux density and forces? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Students must separate each wire's own field from the field acting on it, and apply Newton's third law to the forces.
questions.misconception: Thinking the wire with the larger current experiences the larger force

explanation.body:
If the current in Y is doubled, the B-field at X due to Y doubles. The B-field at Y due to X is unaffected.

The force on X doubles, because the field at X due to Y has doubled. The force on Y also doubles, because the current in Y has doubled. This agrees with Newton's third law.

So the diagram shows $2B_Y$, $B_X$ and $2F$ on each wire.

perOption.A: The forces are a Newton's third law pair, so the force on X must also be $2F$. Also, $B_Y$ should double.
perOption.B: The field at X due to Y should double to $2B_Y$, since Y's current doubled.
perOption.C: $B_X$ depends only on the current in X, so it stays $B_X$. The force on Y must also be $2F$.
perOption.D: Correct. Only Y's field doubles, and both forces double equally.

questions.difficultyReason: Standard application of forces between parallel currents with an inverse-distance comparison.
questions.misconception: Assuming equal and opposite forces on the two sides of the loop cancel

explanation.body:
Parallel wires with currents in opposite directions repel; with currents in the same direction they attract.

PS carries current opposite to XY (repulsion) and QR carries current in the same direction as XY (attraction). Since PS is nearer to XY than QR, the repulsion is greater than the attraction, so the loop moves away from the long wire (to the right).

perOption.A: Assumes the attraction on QR dominates, ignoring that the field is stronger closer to the wire.
perOption.B: Correct. The nearer side PS is repelled more strongly than the farther side QR is attracted.
perOption.C: The forces on PS and QR are both in the plane and perpendicular to XY, and the forces on PQ and SR cancel, so there is no turning effect about an axis parallel to XY.
perOption.D: Assumes the forces on PS and QR cancel, but they differ because the field falls off with distance.
